556.t: From Proto-Indo-European *dwoΗdeḱm̥. Cognates include Sanskrit द्वादश (dvā́daśa) and Latin duodecim.

515.t: From Proto-Hellenic *néwos (compare Mycenaean Greek 𐀚𐀺 (ne-wo)), from Proto-Indo-European *néwos. Cognates include Old English nīewe (English new), Latin novus, Sanskrit नव॑ (náva), and Avestan 𐬥𐬀𐬎𐬎𐬀 (nauua).

555.t: Probably from a Proto-Indo-European *h₃ligos (“indigent, small, needy, ill”). Compare Old Armenian աղքատ (ałkʻat, “poor, indigent”), Old Irish líach (“wretched”), Old Prussian licuts (“small”).

548.t: Unknown; in the absence of an explanation, Beekes prefers a Pre-Greek borrowing, noting that Meier-Brügger's derivation from a Proto-Indo-European *per-trom (“instrument for getting through”) (from *per- (“to go through, fare”) + *-trom (“instrument…

563.t: From ἔκκλητος (ékklētos, “summoned”) + -ία (-ĭ́ā, abstract noun suffix), from ἐκκαλέω (ekkaléō, “to call forth, summon”), from ἐκ (ek) + καλέω (kaléō).

586.t: For *ἄϝις (*áwis, “unseen”), from Proto-Indo-European *n̥wids (“unseen”) equivalent to ἀ- (a-, “un-”) + the root of ἰδεῖν (ideîn) + -ς (-s). The root nominal was remodeled into an α-stem.

500.t: From λογίζομαι (logízomai, “I calculate”) + -μός (-mós, verbal noun suffix).

545.t: Causative reduplication of the root of ἐδάην (edắēn, “learned, taught”, aorist; not attested in the present) with inchoative suffix -σκω (-skō), from Proto-Hellenic *di-dəs-skō, from Proto-Indo-European *dens- (“to learn”).

579.t: Beekes derives it from Pre-Greek, based on its technical semantic domain and lack of resemblance to various Indo-European roots.

584.t: From Proto-Hellenic *ál͏̌l͏̌os, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élyos. Cognates include Latin alius, Old Irish aile, Old Armenian այլ (ayl), Old English elles (English else).

512.t: From Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwr̥̄ḱomt, from earlier *kʷetwr̥-dḱomt (“four-ten”). Cognates include Sanskrit चत्वारिंशत् (catvāriṃśát), Latin quadrāgintā, Old Armenian քառասուն (kʻaṙasun).

521.t: Feminine form of ἀδελφός (ădelphós, “brother”). Displaced the reflex of Proto-Indo-European *swésōr (“sister”), still seen in ἔορ (éor, “daughter of a cousin”), a word found in Hesychius' lexicon.

519.t: From Proto-Hellenic *génos. Cognate with Latin genus, Sanskrit जनस् (jánas), Old Armenian ծին (cin), among others; see also γίγνομαι (gígnomai, “to be born”).

502.t: From the zero-grade of Proto-Indo-European *sem- (“one”). The dative is from the PIE comitative-instrumental.

549.t: From the root of ψεύδω (pseúdō, “to lie”) + -ής (-ḗs, adjective suffix).

571.t: From παιδεύω (paideúō, “rear a child”) + -ία (-íā), from παῖς (paîs, “child”).

504.t: Derived from unattested adverb *πρώ (*prṓ), with locative -ι (-i) as in ἦρι (êrĭ); ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pró (“toward; leading to”).

531.t: From Proto-Hellenic *hwéks, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱs. Cognates include Sanskrit षष् (ṣaṣ), Old Armenian վեց (vecʻ), Latin sex, and Old English six (English six).

574.t: From the root of πλέω (pléō, “to float, sail”) (perhaps in some early meaning of "flow" > "abound") with the suffix -τος (-tos); for the suffix, compare βίοτος (bíotos, “life”), νόστος (nóstos, “journey, return”).

568.t: From Akkadian 𒆳𒆗𒁺 (/⁠Kaldu⁠/), variant of 𒅗𒃻𒁺 (/⁠Kašdu⁠/), either by dissimilation or as a rendering of the Proto-Semitic voiceless lateral fricative *ś.

593.t: Probably a yod-present formation from a Proto-Indo-European *(s)kop- (“to strike, to beat”) (though there is a chance that the word is a substrate borrowing). Compare Proto-Slavic *skopiti (“to castrate”).

572.t: From πέτομαι (pétomai, “to fly”) from Proto-Indo-European *péth₂eti from the root *peth₂- (literally “to spread one’s wings”).

566.t: According to Beekes, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)penh₁- (“to weave, to twist”), with semantic shift "weaving, stretching" > "tensing, strain" > "exertion, toil".

560.t: From στέλλω (stéllō, “to clothe”) + -η (-ē). Compare deverbal English dress.

550.t: From προσεύχομαι (proseúkhomai, “pray”) + -η (-ē, suffix forming action nouns). By surface analysis, προσ- (pros-, “toward”) + εὐχή (eukhḗ, “prayer, wish”).

503.t: Uncertain, though probably connected to and from the same family of words as λοιμός (loimós, “plague”).

569.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kérats, probably remodeled from an earlier s-stem *kéras (like κάρα (kắrā), κάρηνον (kắrēnon), κρανίον (krāníon)), as preserved in e.g. κερασ-φόρος (keras-phóros, “with a horn”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱerh₂- (“head, top; front of…

562.t: From Proto-Hellenic *abnós, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂egʷnós. Cognates include Latin agnus, Old Church Slavonic агнѧ (agnę), Old English ēanian (English yean), and Albanian enjë.

516.t: From ἐν (en, “in”) + δύω (dúō, “to enter”). Compare Latin induo.

577.t: According to Herodotus, a Cyrenaic word; however, more recent research by Solmsen indicates a dialectal Doric origin instead.

507.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ḱe? Proto-Indo-European *ḱómder.? Proto-Indo-European *sem-der.? Proto-Hellenic *ksún Ancient Greek σύν (sún) Ancient Greek συν- (sŭn-) Proto-Indo-European *(s)leh₂gʷ-der.

530.t: Possibly from Proto-Indo-European *welp- (“to hope, expect”), like ἔλπω (élpō, “to cause to hope”).

592.t: Probably related to κρώζω (krṓzō, “I croak”) and κραυγή (kraugḗ, “cry”)

511.t: From πράσσω (prā́ssō, “I do, practice”) + -μα (-mă, result noun suffix).

573.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *pel- Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂g- Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *pl(e)h₂géh₂ Proto-Hellenic *plāgā́ Ancient Greek πληγή From Proto-Hellenic *plāgā́, from Proto-Indo-European *pl(e)h₂géh₂, from *pleh₂g-,…

594.t: From λατρεύς (latreús, “hired servant”) + -εύω (-eúō), the former from λάτρις (látris, “hired servant, handmaid”) + -εύς (-eús).

506.t: From Proto-Indo-European *skh₃tos, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ḱeh₃- (“shadow, darkness”). Cognates include Old Irish scáth, Sanskrit छत्त्र (chattra, “umbrella”), and Old English sceadu (English shadow).

525.t: From Proto-Indo-European *h₁mós; compare ἐμέ (emé, “me”). Cognate with Old Armenian իմ (im).

523.t: From Proto-Indo-European *loykʷós (“remaining, leftover”). Surface analysis λείπω (leípō, “to leave, remain”) + -ός (-ós, deverbal adjective suffix).

501.t: From ἀφ- (aph-, “apo-, away from”) + ἵημι (híēmi, “to send, throw”).

529.t: From προσ- (pros-, “to, toward”) + ἔρχομαι (érkhomai, “to come, go”).

508.t: Uncertain. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰreh₂gʰ- (“to confuse, agitate, disturb”).

533.t: Beekes claims it is of Pre-Greek origin. Probably from δίω.

514.t: From ἐλπίς (elpís, “hope”) + *-ϳω (*-jō). Synchronically also analyzable as ἐλπίς (elpís) + -ίζω (-ízō).

558.t: From πρός (prós, “to, towards, with”) + ἔχω (ékhō, “to have, hold”).

552.t: From ἐκλέγω (eklégō, “to pick out”) + -τός (-tós, adjectival suffix).

588.t: From a root *θ(α)ν (*th(ă)n), with inchoative suffix -σκω (-skō).

564.t: From Proto-Indo-European *tk-éh₁- (“acquisition”), from Proto-Indo-European *tek- (“to take by the hand; to receive, obtain”).

580.t: Formation like σῦριγξ (sûrĭnx) and φόρμιγξ (phórmĭnx). As a word of Mediterranean culture, it remains without Indo-European connection.

570.t: From νεανίας (neanías) (ultimately from νέος (néos, “young, new”)) with the suffix -ίσκος (-ískos), diminutive in form but not necessarily in force.

576.t: With quantitative metathesis of ῆα (êă) to έα (éā), from Proto-Hellenic *stā́wər, from Proto-Indo-European *stéh₂-wr̥, from *steh₂- (“to stand”). Compare πῖαρ (pîar), οὖθαρ (oûthăr).

537.t: Borrowed from a Semitic language, probably from a Canaanite word cognate to Hebrew לְבוֹנָה (ləḇōnā, “frankincense”) and Arabic لُبَان (lubān, “frankincense”), from Proto-West Semitic *laban- (“white”).

536.t: From ἀ- (a-, without) + νόμος (nómos, “law, ordinance; melody”).

520.t: From καθ’ (kath’) + ἅ (há); from κατά (katá) and the neuter plural of ὅς (hós) respectively.

534.t: λειτουργός (leitourgós, “one who performs a λειτουργία, a public servant”) + -έω (-éō, denominative suffix).

513.t: Middle voice from ἐπι- (epi-, “on, upon”) + λανθάνω (lanthánō, “to cause to forget”).
